verses.text: After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed the day of his birth.
Job answered:
“Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.’
Let that day be darkness. Don’t let God from above seek for it, neither let the light shine on it.
Let darkness and the shadow of death claim it for their own. Let a cloud dwell on it. Let all that makes black the day terrify it.
As for that night, let thick darkness seize on it. Let it not rejoice among the days of the year. Let it not come into the number of the months.
Behold, let that night be barren. Let no joyful voice come therein.
Let them curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up leviathan.
Let the stars of its twilight be dark. Let it look for light, but have none, neither let it see the eyelids of the morning,
because it didn’t shut up the doors of my mother’s womb, nor did it hide trouble from my eyes.
“Why didn’t I die from the womb? Why didn’t I give up the spirit when my mother bore me?
Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breast, that I should nurse?
For now should I have lain down and been quiet. I should have slept, then I would have been at rest,
with kings and counselors of the earth, who built up waste places for themselves;
or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver:
or as a hidden untimely birth I had not been, as infants who never saw light.
There the wicked cease from troubling. There the weary are at rest.
There the prisoners are at ease together. They don’t hear the voice of the taskmaster.
The small and the great are there. The servant is free from his master.
“Why is light given to him who is in misery, life to the bitter in soul,
Who long for death, but it doesn’t come; and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,
who rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave?
Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
For my sighing comes before I eat. My groanings are poured out like water.
For the thing which I fear comes on me, That which I am afraid of comes to me.
I am not at ease, neither am I quiet, neither have I rest; but trouble comes.”

footnotes.content: Three friends have sat with Job seven days in silence—the best gift friends can give to the broken. Now his mouth opens, and out spills the agony he can no longer hold. When pain reaches its full weight, sometimes the only honest thing left is to speak what seems unspeakable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job takes his turn to speak—not to answer, but to pour out what no answer yet can fix. His friends listen as he begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In his anguish, Job curses not God but the day of his birth. He wishes the day itself erased, as though undoing that moment might undo all the pain that followed. It's the cry of someone who wishes he'd never had to suffer—which means he wishes he'd never had to live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Job calls for darkness to swallow that day—darkness so complete that even God would not find it or mark it. He longs for his birth to be unmade, forgotten, hidden from the very gaze of heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The day of his birth drowns in shadows and death-darkness in his vision. He wants every brightness stripped away—a poetic reversal of creation, where God said 'Let there be light' and Job now cries 'Let all light be gone.'
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That night should be barren—cut off from the calendar itself, as though it never belonged to any year. It's a real curse formula, familiar to ancient ears: a day so cursed it falls out of time's own reckoning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No joyful voice—no singing, no celebration, no new life born on that night. Job wants that night frozen forever in barrenness and silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let those who curse days—those ancient magicians who stir up the leviathan with their spells—curse this day above all. It's a reference to real practices: Job calls for the night to be subjected to the most powerful curses ancient people knew.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The stars that mark dawn's coming should go dark. That night should seek the light but find none—a reversal of the first creation morning. Job speaks as one who wishes his own first breath had never happened.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His mother's womb should have stayed closed against him—should have kept him from entering a world of suffering. He doesn't blame his mother; he names the thing that broke his heart: life itself brought him trouble he never asked to see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why did I live at all? Why didn't death meet me at birth, before I could know suffering? It's the ache underneath all his curse: he is not angry at his parents but at life itself, which promised nothing and has kept every promise of pain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Why did arms receive him and breasts nurse him? Why was he cared for at all, if only to know this? His question pulls at the oldest tenderness—mother's hands, milk, the first touch of safety—and asks: why this comfort if suffering was always waiting?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: By now he should have lain quiet in death, the only rest that truly lasts. He longs for the sleep from which no pain calls you back awake.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In the grave lie kings and great counselors, sleeping beside their rebuilt ruins. He names the real comfort of that place: no one there builds anymore, strives anymore, rises or falls.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even princes who filled their houses with silver rest there, their treasures worthless now. Death makes all human striving equal—the great and the small, the rich and the poor, all silent together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A stillborn child, never seeing light—Job envies that fate. He sees in the grave not punishment but mercy: those who never lived to suffer are spared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There—in Sheol—the wicked finally stop causing trouble, and the weary finally rest. It's the only hope Job can see: a place where suffering has no power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Prisoners find ease there; no taskmaster's voice cracks the whip. Job pictures the grave as liberation—freedom from the voice of cruelty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Small and great alike, servants free from masters. Death—in Job's telling—is the only true leveler, where every human distinction collapses into silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The deep question: Why does God give life to the bitter soul, the one for whom each day is agony? Why keep someone alive who begs for death?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who long for death dig for it like treasure. The image is stark: desperation so complete that death seems like the prize, the only thing worth seeking.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They rejoice when they find the grave—not in madness, but in relief. Job speaks the darkest truth: for some, death is welcome as salvation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man whose way God has hidden, hedged in on every side—why is he given life? Why must he see at all, if he cannot see where he is going?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before the bread even reaches his mouth, sighing comes first—the body's first response. His sorrow fills him before hunger does, spills from him like water he cannot contain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What we fear most has a way of finding us. Readers today hear an echo in this verse: our deepest anxieties, the things we dread in darkness, often teach us that God's hand remains even in fear—though Job cannot see it yet, and neither can we.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No rest, no quiet, no peace—only trouble, relentless and dark. Job's chapter ends as it began: a cry from the pit, the cry of a man who cannot escape his own mind.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
